spark.summary: Content-Defined Chunking uses a rolling hash (Rabin fingerprint) to slice files at content-dependent boundaries so byte insertions only invalidate the modified chunk instead of shifting every downstream block.
spark.keyTakeaway: To bound blast radius during partial cluster failures, fixed-size chunking suffers from the boundary-shift problem; CDC with a rolling hash + SHA-256 deduplication achieves true O(delta) uploads across multi-gigabyte files.
spark.byteSummary:
If you split a 1 GB file into fixed 4 MB blocks and insert 10 bytes at the very beginning, every single byte shifts right by 10 positions. All 250 blocks change their SHA-256 hashes, forcing a full 1 GB re-upload.

Content-Defined Chunking (CDC) eliminates this boundary-shift problem. A sliding window (e.g., 48 bytes) computes a fast rolling hash such as a Rabin fingerprint or Gear hash (FastCDC) as it scans the file. Whenever the hash's lowest bits match a target mask (e.g., `hash & 0x1FFF == 0`), it places a chunk boundary.

Because boundaries depend on local byte patterns rather than absolute offsets, inserting 10 bytes at the start only alters the first chunk; all remaining 249 chunks match their existing SHA-256 hashes in S3 and are skipped during upload.

learningJourney.title: The Fixed-Chunk Boundary-Shift Problem
learningJourney.purpose: Observe why naive 4 MB fixed-size splitting fails on prepend or mid-file edits.

explanation.foundation: Fixed-size chunking slices a file at offsets `0, 4MB, 8MB, ...`.
explanation.core: If a user prepends a 1 KB header to a 100 MB VM image or video project, every downstream 4 MB boundary shifts by 1 KB.
explanation.deepDive: Every chunk's SHA-256 digest changes, destroying deduplication and wasting 100 MB of upload bandwidth.

learningJourney.title: Rolling Hash Mechanics (Rabin Fingerprint & FastCDC)
learningJourney.purpose: Compute content-dependent cut points in O(1) per byte using a sliding window.

explanation.foundation: Think of **Rolling Hash Mechanics (Rabin Fingerprint & FastCDC)** as the intuition layer for Content-Defined Chunking (CDC) & Cross-Device Delta Sync: Compute content-dependent cut points in O(1) per byte using a sliding window.
explanation.core: Instead of re-hashing a 48-byte window from scratch at each byte, a rolling hash updates the hash in O(1) arithmetic when the window slides by 1 byte (`out_byte` leaves, `in_byte` enters). Modern FastCDC uses a Gear hash lookup table to scan at >1 GB/sec on a single CPU core.
explanation.deepDive: Under heavy load or partial failure, rolling hash mechanics (rabin fingerprint & fastcdc) becomes a critical lever for predictable latency and correctness. Production CDC pairs FastCDC with grace-period mark-and-sweep GC, tenant-isolated KMS keys, and optimistic revision conflict forks.

sectionDiagram.title: O(1) Sliding Rolling Hash

cards.label: 1+ GB/s Speed
cards.detail: Gear hashing avoids modular division, running near memory-copy speed.

cards.label: Local Anchoring
cards.detail: Cut points depend only on the surrounding ~48 bytes.

sectionDiagram.summary: A rolling hash finds content-anchored boundaries in a single linear O(N) pass.
sectionDiagram.caption: FastCDC slides a Gear rolling hash across bytes to place boundaries based on local content.

decisionFramework.problem: How to implement Content-Defined Chunking (CDC) & Cross-Device Delta Sync without hitting unbounded tail latency, state divergence, or operational fragility.
decisionFramework.naiveSolution: Use a single unpartitioned path with unbounded retries and synchronous global coordination.
decisionFramework.whyItFails: Global coordination serializes throughput under load, while unbounded retries amplify transient stalls into full outages.
decisionFramework.alternatives: Compare synchronous strict-consistency paths against bounded asynchronous replication, local caching, or partitioned ownership.
decisionFramework.decision: To bound blast radius during partial cluster failures, fixed-size chunking suffers from the boundary-shift problem; CDC with a rolling hash + SHA-256 deduplication achieves true O(delta) uploads across multi-gigabyte files.
decisionFramework.tradeOffs: Gains predictable p99 latency and fault isolation in exchange for explicit bounding, observability, and slightly higher implementation complexity.

learningJourney.title: Min/Max Chunk Clamping & Normalized Chunking
learningJourney.purpose: Prevent pathological tiny (1-byte) or huge (100 MB) chunks by enforcing `[min_size, max_size]` bounds.

explanation.foundation: Think of **Min/Max Chunk Clamping & Normalized Chunking** as the intuition layer for Content-Defined Chunking (CDC) & Cross-Device Delta Sync: Prevent pathological tiny (1-byte) or huge (100 MB) chunks by enforcing `[min_size, max_size]` bounds.
explanation.core: A raw random bitmask follows a geometric distribution, occasionally producing 10-byte chunks (metadata explosion) or 50 MB chunks (poor dedup). Enforcing `min_size` (e.g., 2 MB) skips hash checks until `min_size` bytes are read, while `max_size` (e.g., 8 MB) forces a cut, keeping chunk counts and metadata predictable.
explanation.deepDive: Under heavy load or partial failure, min/max chunk clamping & normalized chunking becomes a critical lever for predictable latency and correctness. Production CDC pairs FastCDC with grace-period mark-and-sweep GC, tenant-isolated KMS keys, and optimistic revision conflict forks.

learningJourney.codeExample:
def validate_chunk_bounds(chunk_len: int, min_sz: int, max_sz: int) -> bool:
    return min_sz <= chunk_len <= max_sz

sectionDiagram.title: Bounded Chunk Size Distribution

cards.label: Metadata Bound
cards.detail: min_size guarantees at most N / min_size chunk entries.

cards.label: FastCDC Trick
cards.detail: Using a stricter mask before avg_size narrows variance.

sectionDiagram.summary: Clamping chunk sizes between `min_size` and `max_size` bounds both metadata overhead and tail upload size.
sectionDiagram.caption: Skipping checks below min_size and forcing cuts at max_size stabilizes chunk sizes.

learningJourney.title: SHA-256 Content-Addressable Storage & Delta Negotiation
learningJourney.purpose: Check which chunk hashes already exist on the server before uploading any binary payload.

explanation.foundation: Think of **SHA-256 Content-Addressable Storage & Delta Negotiation** as the intuition layer for Content-Defined Chunking (CDC) & Cross-Device Delta Sync: Check which chunk hashes already exist on the server before uploading any binary payload.
explanation.core: After slicing a file into CDC chunks, the client computes each chunk's SHA-256 digest and sends the ordered hash list (`[h1, h2', h3, h4]`) to the Block Service. The server checks its chunk index and returns only missing hashes (`[h2']`), cutting upload traffic by >90% on incremental edits.
explanation.deepDive: Under heavy load or partial failure, sha-256 content-addressable storage & delta negotiation becomes a critical lever for predictable latency and correctness. Production CDC pairs FastCDC with grace-period mark-and-sweep GC, tenant-isolated KMS keys, and optimistic revision conflict forks.

sectionDiagram.title: Hash-First Delta Negotiation

cards.label: Content-Addressable
cards.detail: Chunks are stored at `blocks/{sha256}`—identical chunks across files share 1 copy.

cards.label: Bandwidth Win
cards.detail: Editing 1 slide in a 500 MB deck uploads ~4 MB instead of 500 MB.

sectionDiagram.summary: Negotiating SHA-256 manifests before uploading ensures only genuinely new chunks cross the wire.
sectionDiagram.caption: The client sends chunk hashes first and uploads only the modified chunk h2' to S3.

learningJourney.title: Chunk Compression, Convergent vs. Per-Tenant Encryption
learningJourney.purpose: Balance storage deduplication against zero-knowledge tenant encryption.

explanation.foundation: Think of **Chunk Compression, Convergent vs. Per-Tenant Encryption** as the intuition layer for Content-Defined Chunking (CDC) & Cross-Device Delta Sync: Balance storage deduplication against zero-knowledge tenant encryption.
explanation.core: Cross-user deduplication requires identical plaintext chunks to produce identical ciphertext (convergent encryption using `HMAC(chunk_hash, chunk)`), which can leak whether another user owns a known file. Enterprise systems therefore scope deduplication per `tenant_id` using per-tenant KMS keys and Zstd compression per chunk.
explanation.deepDive: Under heavy load or partial failure, chunk compression, convergent vs. per-tenant encryption becomes a critical lever for predictable latency and correctness. Production CDC pairs FastCDC with grace-period mark-and-sweep GC, tenant-isolated KMS keys, and optimistic revision conflict forks.

learningJourney.codeExample:
def compress_chunk(raw: bytes) -> bytes:
    import zlib
    compressed = zlib.compress(raw, level=3)
    return compressed if len(compressed) < len(raw) else raw

sectionDiagram.title: Per-Tenant Encryption & Zstd

cards.label: Skip Incompressible
cards.detail: JPEG/MP4 chunks skip compression to save CPU.

cards.label: Privacy Boundary
cards.detail: Per-tenant keys prevent cross-org hash-oracle side channels.

sectionDiagram.summary: Per-tenant encryption and conditional compression protect privacy without sacrificing org-level dedup.
sectionDiagram.caption: Compressing and encrypting chunks with tenant-scoped keys prevents cross-tenant leakage.

learningJourney.title: Reference Counting & Safe Orphan Chunk Garbage Collection
learningJourney.purpose: Delete unreferenced S3 chunks safely without racing against concurrent uploads or file restores.

explanation.foundation: Because multiple file versions share chunk `h1`, deleting a file cannot immediately delete `h1` from S3.
explanation.core: A naive `ref_count == 0` delete races with an in-flight upload that just skipped `h1` during negotiation.
explanation.deepDive: Production systems use a two-phase mark-and-sweep GC with a 7-day grace period (`unreferenced_since`) and soft-delete locks.

sectionDiagram.title: Two-Phase Grace-Period GC

cards.label: TOCTOU Fix
cards.detail: Grace window + row lock prevents deleting a chunk while a client is referencing it.

cards.label: Version History
cards.detail: 30-day file undo keeps chunk references alive until snapshot expiry.

sectionDiagram.summary: Grace-period mark-and-sweep GC prevents race conditions when reclaiming unreferenced blocks.
sectionDiagram.caption: A 7-day grace window and row lock prevent GC from deleting chunks mid-upload.

learningJourney.title: Version Vectors & Cross-Device Conflict Forks
learningJourney.purpose: Detect concurrent offline edits across devices and preserve both copies without data loss.

explanation.foundation: If Laptop A and Laptop B both edit `budget.xlsx` while offline, neither should silently overwrite the other.
explanation.core: Each file carries a monotonic `revision_id` and parent pointer.
explanation.deepDive: When Laptop B reconnects with `base_rev=5` while the server is at `rev=6`, the Metadata Service rejects the overwrite and forks `budget (Laptop B's conflicted copy).xlsx`.

sectionDiagram.title: Optimistic Revision & Conflict Fork

cards.label: Zero Silent Loss
cards.detail: Conflicting offline edits are preserved as separate files.

cards.label: Fast Sync
cards.detail: The forked file still reuses all unchanged CDC chunks in S3.

sectionDiagram.summary: Optimistic revision checks detect offline edit races and create safe conflict copies.
sectionDiagram.caption: When two devices edit offline, a revision mismatch triggers a conflict-copy fork.

options.text: CDC compresses the 2 GB file into 50 bytes.
options.feedback: CDC slices files into chunks; it does not compress 2 GB into 50 bytes.

options.text: CDC places boundaries using a rolling hash of local byte patterns, so only the first chunk changes while downstream chunks keep identical hashes.
options.feedback: Correct! Content-anchored boundaries re-synchronize immediately after the edit, preserving deduplication for all remaining chunks.
Fixed chunking can use SHA-256, but every block's content shifts.

options.text: CDC skips uploading metadata to the server.
options.feedback: The client still sends the updated chunk manifest.

knowledgeChecks.explanation: Rolling-hash boundaries depend on local byte windows, isolating insertions to the edited chunk.

knowledgeChecks.question: What is the purpose of enforcing `min_size` and `max_size` bounds in FastCDC?

options.text: To guarantee every chunk has the exact same byte length.
options.feedback: CDC chunks are variable-sized between min_size and max_size.

options.text: To prevent tiny-chunk metadata explosion and cap worst-case chunk transfer size.
options.feedback: Correct! Clamping bounds the number of chunk records per file and caps individual block sizes.

options.text: To disable SHA-256 hashing on large files.
options.feedback: Every chunk is still hashed with SHA-256.

options.text: To force all files to be multiples of 4 MB.
options.feedback: Files keep their exact original length.

knowledgeChecks.explanation: Clamping `[min_size, max_size]` eliminates the extreme tails of a geometric rolling-hash distribution.

knowledgeChecks.question: Why is immediate `DELETE` on `ref_count == 0` dangerous in content-addressable chunk storage?

options.text: S3 charges extra for immediate deletes.
options.feedback: The issue is correctness, not delete pricing.

options.text: An in-flight upload that just saw `chunk_hash` as existing may commit a new file referencing that chunk right as GC deletes it.
options.feedback: Correct! A grace window + row lock prevents TOCTOU races between GC and concurrent uploads.
SHA-256 digests are deterministic and never expire.

options.text: It breaks client-side SQLite file watchers.
options.feedback: Local watchers do not manage server-side S3 GC.

knowledgeChecks.explanation: Two-phase GC with a grace period prevents deleting a block that a concurrent upload is about to reference.

beginner.summary: Content-Defined Chunking splits large files at content patterns so editing one part only uploads the changed piece.
beginner.keyTakeaway: To bound blast radius during partial cluster failures, fixed-size chunking suffers from the boundary-shift problem; CDC with a rolling hash + SHA-256 deduplication achieves true O(delta) uploads across multi-gigabyte files.
beginner.byteSummary: If you cut a file every 4 MB strictly by position, adding one word at the top shifts everything and forces a full re-upload. CDC uses a sliding fingerprint to cut at natural byte patterns so unchanged pieces are recognized and skipped.

advanced.keyTakeaway: To bound blast radius during partial cluster failures, fixed-size chunking suffers from the boundary-shift problem; CDC with a rolling hash + SHA-256 deduplication achieves true O(delta) uploads across multi-gigabyte files.
